reviews.pullQuote: A2UI treats UI as validated data, not code — and ships first-party renderers for React, Flutter, SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose from one catalog.
reviews.testimonial: I'd build on A2UI. Its catalog model — a JSON Schema the agent must compose within, with no executable code crossing the trust boundary — plus the catalog-agnostic accessibility requirements that force `@accessibility` attributes onto ARIA, Flutter Semantics and iOS/Android accessibility APIs, is the only architecture here that gives me one agent and one component vocabulary across web and native. The honest trade-off against Ouro UI, which I seriously considered: Ouro is the better *design system* for the dual audience, because it also covers the agent-operated side (CLI, MCP, App Intents) with machine-checked claims, while A2UI gives me a protocol and a Basic Catalog and expects me to bring my own styled components. I accept that: I'd rather own the visual layer than own the protocol, and A2UI's Compose renderer still trailing at v0.9.1 is a gap I can live with when the Flutter, SwiftUI and web renderers are at v1.0.
reviews.evaluations:
**A2UI** — The architecture I'd bet on: UI is expressed as validated data against a catalog JSON Schema, never executable code, so an untrusted or remote agent can only compose components you granted it. The spec defines four agent→renderer messages (`createSurface`, `updateComponents`, `updateDataModel`, `deleteSurface`), JSON-Pointer data-model updates for progressive streaming, and — crucially for my purposes — [catalog-agnostic accessibility requirements](https://a2ui.org/specification/v1.0-a2ui/) that *mandate* mapping `@accessibility` to WAI-ARIA, Flutter `Semantics`, and iOS/Android accessibility APIs, with explicit labels overriding inferred ones. First-party renderers exist for React, Lit, Angular, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose, with conformance YAML suites for anyone writing a new one ([SDK matrix](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/)). Observed gaps, not guesses: the Compose/AndroidX renderer is still listed at v0.9.1 while the others are v1.0, and A2UI is a protocol plus a Basic Catalog — it deliberately defers styling to the host framework's theme, so you still need a component library underneath. Apache-2.0, Google-originated, maintained in a separate `a2ui-project` org. What would settle my remaining doubt: a v1.0 Compose renderer and more non-Google production catalogs shipped publicly.

**Ouro UI** — The closest thing here to an answer to the literal brief, and my runner-up. It splits explicitly into Ouro HX (React components installed via the shadcn CLI, built on Base UI, reading shadcn theme variables) and Ouro AX (a conformance standard plus an "X-ray" that calls a CLI/HTTP/MCP surface from outside and checks it against claims like "ambiguous verbs don't act" and "commands other people see refuse to run without `--why`"), with a one-action model that generates CLI, MCP, WebMCP, web control, App Intent, SwiftUI button and Reins surfaces from a single declaration ([parity table](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/apple/)). It also ships `A2UISurface` and `OuroMcpApp` components, so it composes with rather than competes against the protocols. The objections are concrete and published by the project itself: the Apple half is 0.5.0 pre-1.0 with five SwiftUI components, Android and Windows are "open for a builder," and the parity table's own cells read "Not yet" for `text.reflows` on web. Adoption also appears nascent — the showcases are the author's own apps (Spoonjoy, Ouro MD). A 1.0 Apple package with component parity, and two or three third-party adopters, would move this to first place for me.

**MCP Apps** — Now a stable extension (SEP-1865, status Stable 2026-01-26) with a genuinely good security model: `ui://` resources, mandatory iframe sandboxing, server-declared CSP `connectDomains`/`resourceDomains`/`frameDomains` and opt-in permissions, and JSON-RPC bidirectional messaging to the host ([spec](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx)). It's the right distribution layer if your goal is rendering inside ChatGPT, Claude, VS Code and Goose. But the initial content type is `text/html;profile=mcp-app` — it's web-in-an-iframe by construction, with no native rendering path — and it's a transport plus host contract, not a design system. I'd use it alongside my choice, not instead of it.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — Architecturally the sharpest idea on the agent-operation side: `defineAction` declares a capability once with a Zod schema, and it becomes an agent tool, a React `useActionQuery` call, an HTTP route, an MCP tool, an A2A endpoint and a CLI command, all sharing one validation and permission path ([README](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native)). That's the correct answer to "both people and agents use it." The trade-off is scope: it's a full opinionated application framework — PostgreSQL/PGlite, Nitro hosting, its own auth, chat, memory, automations — so adopting it is an architecture decision, not a UI decision, and it's React/web only. If I were greenfield on web and wanted the whole stack, this would be a serious contender.

**CopilotKit** — The strongest *integration* story: AG-UI 1.0 as the agent–user event protocol, plus shared state, human-in-the-loop, frontend tools, and renderers for React, Angular, Vue, React Native, Slack and Teams — and it now speaks A2UI 1.0 and renders sandboxed MCP Apps ([README](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit)). So it's a consumer of my pick rather than a rival to it. My hesitation is that it's a chat/agent-surface layer with a commercial product (Intelligence, Soar) attached, not a design system: the visual components are chat primitives and slots, and its native coverage is React Native, not SwiftUI/Compose. If I needed to wire an existing LangGraph or Mastra agent to a React app tomorrow, I'd reach for it.

**json-render** — Impressively broad: one catalog of Zod-typed components renders to React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, React Native, Next.js routes, Remotion video, react-pdf, email, Ink terminals and even R3F scenes, with a flat `root` + `elements` spec format and 36 prebuilt shadcn components ([README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render)). Conceptually it's A2UI's twin for the web/JS world. Two things decided it against A2UI for me: every target is a JavaScript runtime — React Native is the closest thing to "native," with no SwiftUI or Compose renderer — and it's a Vercel Labs project with no published wire specification or cross-language conformance suite, so a Python or Swift agent isn't a first-class participant. A versioned spec and a non-JS renderer would change my read.

**Vercel UI SDK** — The most interesting *primitive* design here: `definePrimitive` with state, api, and slots, where keyboard navigation, focus recovery, popups, selection, typeahead and ARIA live in framework-agnostic `@ui-sdk/core` and compile to parts for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Components ([README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui)). The README is explicit that humans aren't expected to author this — "your agents will" — which is a real stance on agent-authored UI, distinct from agent-rendered UI. It's labelled beta under Vercel beta terms, there's no native target, and it gives you behaviors rather than a design system or an agent protocol. I'd watch it; I wouldn't standardize on a beta behavior layer for a cross-platform agent product yet.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — A tight, well-scoped design system: Tailwind 4 token integration, Radix-based accessible components, `AppsSDKUIProvider` for router links, semantic utilities like `text-secondary`/`bg-surface` so your app inherits ChatGPT's surface treatment ([README](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui)). If ChatGPT is your distribution channel, this is the correct skin. It is explicitly a skin for one host, though — React 18/19 plus Tailwind 4, web only, no native, no agent-operation surface beyond what the Apps SDK itself provides. Nothing here is wrong; the scope just doesn't match "across web and native platforms."

**AI Elements** — I have to disqualify this on the project's own evidence: the README carries a deprecation warning saying it moves to shadcn/ui and will be deprecated at the end of November 2026 ([README](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements)). The components themselves (Conversation, Message, Reasoning, code blocks) are good and are being absorbed — I found them already listed under AI Elements in the shadcn docs sidebar. Use the shadcn-hosted version; don't start here.

**shadcn/ui** — The distribution mechanism is the real asset, and it's the most agent-legible one in this list: `registry.json` items, namespaced third-party registries in `components.json`, and an official MCP server so an assistant can browse, search and install components by name ([MCP docs](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/mcp)). Its docs now also carry AI Elements and a Skills section. Two limits for this brief: copy-in source means you own the upgrade burden (the Ouro README's multi-page upgrade notes are a vivid illustration of what that costs downstream), and it's React/web only with no native target and no protocol for agent-composed UI. It's the substrate I'd expect my web half to sit on — which is exactly where Ouro HX sits.

**Base UI** — Reached stable v1.0 in December 2025 and is shipping monthly; v1.9.0 added menu filtering and large-list mount performance work, Drawer went stable in 1.3.0, OTPField in 1.6.0 ([releases](https://base-ui.com/react/overview/releases)). Unstyled, composable, from the people who built Radix, Floating UI and Material UI, with a `CSPProvider` and documented `llms.txt`. As a foundation for the human-facing web layer it's my default recommendation. It is, by design, not a design system, has no agent-facing concept, and is React-only — so it's a component in my answer, not the answer.

**Radix UI** — Still the reference implementation of composable, accessible unstyled primitives, and the reason shadcn/ui and OpenAI's Apps SDK UI both exist in their current form ([README](https://github.com/radix-ui/primitives)). Note the license line: MIT, copyright WorkOS, and the original authors now list themselves on the Base UI team. That's not abandonment, but if I were starting fresh in late 2026 I'd pick Base UI over Radix for the same architectural role. Either way: React-only, no native, no agent surface.

**MUI** — A decade of battle-testing, an enormous component surface extended by MUI X, and a genuinely comprehensive migration history ([README](https://github.com/mui/material-ui)). If I were building an internal tool for people and bolting on an agent later, this is a defensible, low-risk choice. For this brief it's the wrong shape: it's an opinionated Material Design implementation for React with no native target, no schema-constrained generative path, and nothing that makes its component semantics legible to an agent. Notably, the same org's newer bet is Base UI.

**Fluent UI** — The README itself states v9 is shipping its final stable release, and the repo houses three concurrent projects (v9 React, v8 React, Web Components) with a documented migration path between them ([README](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui)). Griffel-based styling and real theming depth, used across Microsoft 365, Office and Edge. For a Microsoft-ecosystem product it's the right call. For mine, the three-generation split is a tax, there's no native mobile story in this repo, and the font/icon assets carry a separate license agreement — and again, no agent-facing layer.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — The deepest accessibility and internationalization engineering in the list: WAI-ARIA APG conformance, 30+ languages, RTL, date/number formatting via the `@internationalized` packages, and a three-layer split (Spectrum / Aria / Stately) where React Stately is explicitly usable on non-web platforms like React Native ([README](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum)). If my criterion were "most rigorous behavior layer," this wins outright. It isn't a cross-platform design system — React Spectrum is Adobe's visual language — and there's no agent protocol here. I'd happily build an A2UI catalog *on top of* React Aria for the web renderer.

**Chakra UI** — Pleasant DX, RSC-compatible, and notable for shipping an MCP server (`@chakra-ui/react-mcp`) prominently in the README, which is a real nod to agent-assisted authoring ([README](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui)). But that MCP server helps an agent *write code with* Chakra; it doesn't make the running interface agent-operable. Emotion-based, React/web only, no native target. Good library; not an answer to this question.

**Tamagui** — The most credible shared-code story for web + React Native: an optimizing compiler that flattens styled components to a `div` with atomic CSS on web and a `View` with hoisted styles on native, with concrete numbers in the README (49 of ~55 inline styled components flattened; ~15% Lighthouse gain) ([README](https://github.com/tamagui/tamagui)). If "native" means React Native for me, this is the strongest candidate. Two reservations: the compiler is a significant build-system commitment and a debugging surface of its own, and "native" here stops at React Native — no SwiftUI or Compose — with nothing addressing agents.

**Flutter** — A single codebase to mobile, web, desktop and embedded, with Impeller/Skia rendering, both Material and Cupertino widget sets, and real pixel control ([README](https://github.com/flutter/flutter)). It's also a first-class A2UI target: `a2ui_flutter` is at v1.0 and Dart has all three SDK layers, so an all-Dart app can run inference and rendering in one project. That's precisely why I treat Flutter as a *platform under* my choice rather than as the choice: by itself it offers no agent-facing contract, and the owned-pixel approach means you opt out of native platform widgets and their accessibility behaviors.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — The strongest native quality ceiling, period: declarative views across iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, visionOS and watchOS, with accessibility, Liquid Glass adoption guidance and deep UIKit/AppKit interop documented in the framework reference ([SwiftUI docs](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui)). On Apple platforms the agent surface is App Intents, not SwiftUI itself — which is exactly the seam Ouro AX and Apple's own ecosystem exploit. I can't choose it for this brief because it covers one vendor's platforms and nothing on the web, but any serious cross-platform answer must render well *here*, and A2UI's SwiftUI renderer is at v1.0.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — Material 3 in Compose gives you dynamic color, a full component set and a theming system with documented migration from M2, inside a mature declarative framework with strong accessibility semantics and testing APIs ([Android docs](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3)). Google also publishes `androidx.a2ui` and `material3-a2ui` artifacts, so Compose is a real A2UI target — though, as noted, currently at protocol v0.9.1 rather than v1.0. As with SwiftUI, it's a platform I'd render *into*, not a cross-platform answer: Android-first, with no web story and no agent contract of its own.
candidateOrder: SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines

reviews.evaluations:
**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — One defineAction (zod schema) becomes an agent tool, a React hook, and HTTP, MCP, A2A and CLI endpoints. Shared actions, data and UI state suit apps used by people and agents together. It is an application framework, not a design system, and the README shows no native renderer. Native rendering would address that objection. [README](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native)

**MUI** — The README describes a React implementation of Material Design, with MUI X for advanced components. The README shows no agent protocol and no native target. It is a good human-facing widget set to place behind an agent catalog. [README](https://github.com/mui/material-ui)

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — Apple's docs describe a declarative UI framework for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, visionOS and watchOS, with an accessibility section. It is Apple-only, so it can't cover web alone. A2UI lists SwiftUI as a renderer target, which makes it a good native backend. I did not verify the HIG pages separately. [Docs](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui)

**MCP Apps** — Tools declare ui:// HTML resources that render in sandboxed iframes in hosts such as Claude, ChatGPT and VS Code. The wire protocol is unchanged between 1.x and 2.x, and agent skills ship for scaffolding. It is chat-host-centric and web-only, and host support varies. [README](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps)

**A2UI** — Chosen. UI is expressed as data, validated against a schema, and limited to a catalog the app developer approves. The layers are inference, transport, and rendering through a core library, a framework adapter and a catalog. It ships Python SDKs for ADK and A2A, and TypeScript renderers for Lit, Angular and React. The README names Flutter, SwiftUI and Compose as target frameworks. Observed gaps: no visual design system, and some packages are marked "Not published yet". [README](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui)

**Fluent UI** — The README describes React v9, React v8 and Web Components projects. Edge uses the Web Components project and Microsoft 365 uses v9. It is accessible and themeable, but the README shows no agent or native layer. It could supply catalog widgets for a web renderer. [README](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui)

**Ouro UI** — It splits into HX for people and AX for agents. It has shadcn-registry React components built on Base UI, and a screen check covering accessibility and layout. Declared actions generate a CLI, MCP and WebMCP tools, plus Apple App Intents. The Apple half has not reached a stable version, Android and Windows are open for a builder, and the project is young. It is the closest philosophical match and my strong second choice. [README](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui)

**Flutter** — One codebase compiles to mobile, web and desktop, with Material and Cupertino widgets. A2UI has a Flutter adapter, so Flutter works well as a rendering host. The README shows no agent protocol. [README](https://github.com/flutter/flutter)

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — Material 3 components and theming for Compose. The page also points to Android agent tooling. It is Android-focused rather than cross-platform. A2UI lists Compose as a target. [Docs](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3)

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — React Aria is unstyled accessible components, and React Stately is state hooks. The README says Stately can be used on other platforms such as React Native. Strong foundation for human users; the README shows no agent layer. [README](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum)

**CopilotKit** — Agent-UI stack with chat components, generative UI, shared state, human-in-the-loop and the AG-UI protocol. The README says it supports A2UI specs and MCP Apps, and it targets React, Angular, Vue, React Native, Slack and Teams. It is a runtime and chat layer, not a design system, and it promotes a commercial Intelligence product. It complements A2UI. [README](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit)

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — Tailwind 4 tokens and Radix-based React components tuned for ChatGPT apps. It is web-only and tied to the ChatGPT host. [README](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui)

**Chakra UI** — Accessible React components, and the README includes an MCP server install link. It is web-only React, and I saw no native renderer. [README](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui)

**json-render** — A zod-defined catalog constrains the AI, specs stream progressively, and it has renderers for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and React Native. It also ships 36 shadcn components and an MCP package. It is very close to A2UI, but I saw no Flutter, SwiftUI or Compose renderers in the README. It would be my pick for a project limited to web and React Native. [README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render)

**Vercel UI SDK** — Framework-agnostic behaviors (focus, selection, popups, ARIA) in @ui-sdk/core, with adapters for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Components, designed for agents to write. It is beta and has no native renderer. [README](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui)

**AI Elements** — The README warns that the project will be deprecated at the end of November 2026 and replaced by a shadcn/ui version. It is chat components over shadcn/ui and the AI SDK. I would not start new work on it. [README](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements)

**Radix UI** — Low-level accessible React primitives for design systems. Web-only, with no agent features in the README. [README](https://github.com/radix-ui/primitives)

**Base UI** — Unstyled accessible components from the Radix, Floating UI and Material UI creators. Ouro HX builds on it. It is web-only. [README](https://github.com/mui/base-ui)

**shadcn/ui** — Open-code components meant as a base for your own library. Ouro and json-render build on it, so it is a good widget source for an A2UI catalog. It is web-only. [README](https://github.com/shadcn-ui/ui)

**Tamagui** — A style library and compiler that shares code across React and React Native. It flattens styled components to a div plus atomic CSS on web, or a View on native. It suits a universal human-facing UI. The README mentions no agent protocol. [README](https://github.com/tamagui/tamagui)
reviews.pullQuote: A2UI sends agents' interfaces as schema-validated data, never code, and renders them with native components across web and mobile.
reviews.testimonial: I chose A2UI because the agent sends validated JSON instead of executable code, and an app-controlled widget catalog limits what it can compose. Its renderers cover React, Angular, Lit and Flutter, and the README names SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose as targets. The trade-off is that it is not a visual design system, so I would still need shadcn/ui, Material or Fluent for the catalog widgets. It is also young, with some packages marked as not yet published. I accept that over the chat-host lock-in of Apps SDK UI or MCP Apps.
candidateOrder: SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines

reviews.pullQuote: I’d choose A2UI for its catalog-constrained agent interface and native renderers, keeping platform conventions without handing agents arbitrary executable UI.
reviews.testimonial: I would choose A2UI as the shared interface contract across web and native, rather than force every platform into one component implementation. Catalogs, incremental updateComponents messages, and callRendererFunction give me explicit boundaries for agent composition, live updates, and permitted interaction. I particularly value allowedCallers and requiresUserActivation because human gestures and autonomous requests should not carry identical authority. Ouro UI offers more explicit consent classes and generated action surfaces, which I would miss, but A2UI’s documented web, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose renderer coverage better matches my platform requirements.
reviews.evaluations:
**Vercel UI SDK** — This is substantially more than documentation for coding agents: its framework-free behavior core supports five web adapters, while `createAgent`, `snapshot`, and `act` expose live component state and invoke the same component APIs used by people. The bridge supports approval callbacks and agent-origin change cancellation; its source also makes the DOM dependency clear. I would shortlist it for an agent-operable web design system, but its documented adapters do not supply native SwiftUI, Compose, or React Native rendering, and the project remains beta. Native adapters and cross-platform interaction tests would address my main objection. [Agent architecture](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/llms.txt), [bridge source](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui/blob/724a7d6c2d0ca1251a8eb6172462ae220c484714/packages/core/src/page/agent/agent.ts).

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — I particularly like the separation between unstyled React Aria behavior, React Stately state, and Spectrum’s finished design system. Documented screen-reader testing, normalized press interactions, localized strings, and international date handling make this a strong human-facing web foundation; meaningful semantics also help accessibility-tree-based automation, although that is not a dedicated agent action contract. React Stately can be reused on native, but that does not make the DOM-based controls native components. I would add a native presentation layer and explicit authorized domain tools rather than mistake state portability for complete platform coverage. [Architecture and library boundaries](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum), [accessibility and interaction details](https://react-aria.adobe.com/quality#accessibility).

**shadcn/ui** — Its architectural advantage is source ownership: components are distributed through a registry and CLI, and their top-level implementation becomes application code. The MCP server gives coding agents registry search and installation, not automatic permission to operate the finished application. That makes customization straightforward but leaves my team responsible for integrating upstream changes, maintaining accessibility after edits, and implementing native equivalents and runtime actions. I would happily use it inside a web renderer catalog; a shared action contract and tested native implementations would be needed before making it the cross-platform foundation. [Open-code architecture](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs), [MCP’s actual scope](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/mcp).

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — SwiftUI provides declarative views, model-to-view data flow, adaptive Apple controls, and accessibility integration; the HIG supplies platform-specific design guidance rather than a portable component runtime. Importantly, Apple also has a genuine structured agent-facing path through App Intents, exposing actions and entities to Apple Intelligence, Siri, Shortcuts, and other system experiences. I would strongly favor this combination for an Apple-only product, but it does not supply my web or Android interface. Shared backend operations plus separate platform implementations would solve reach at the cost of maintaining multiple presentation stacks. [SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui), [HIG](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines), [App Intents](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appintents).

**Fluent UI** — The web repository contains distinct React v9, React v8, and Web Components implementations; v9’s provider/theme setup gives a concrete enterprise UI foundation. Native is not absent: FluentUI React Native is a separate customizable implementation, but its fetched README explicitly labels all four listed platforms alpha and warns about platform differences. I therefore would not assume one production-ready component contract spans web and native, or that a Fluent-styled copilot supplies a shared agent action layer. Proven component parity, stable native coverage, and explicit runtime tool bindings would materially improve its fit. [Web project boundaries](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui), [native implementation and status](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui-react-native).

**Base UI** — Its unstyled React parts handle ARIA, keyboard navigation, and focus while leaving visual design to the application. The `render` composition mechanism merges behavior onto a custom element, but requires correct ref forwarding and prop spreading—an important constraint when people or agents customize wrappers. I consider it a strong web catalog implementation, not a native renderer or agent protocol. I would supply tokens, visible focus styling, authorized application actions, and separate native implementations; those are additional layers rather than defects in Base UI’s stated scope. [Composition contract](https://base-ui.com/react/handbook/composition), [accessibility responsibilities](https://base-ui.com/react/overview/accessibility).

**MUI** — Material UI offers a comprehensive React implementation of Material Design, with MUI X extending it for complex interfaces. Its supported-platform contract is browser-oriented, and its MCP server provides official documentation and examples to coding assistants rather than exposing the application’s business operations. I would choose it for a conventional React administration product, but would still have to bridge native presentation and agent execution myself. A constrained renderer catalog around MUI and shared authorized handlers would address the agent side; native controls remain a separate implementation. [Repository architecture](https://github.com/mui/material-ui), [supported platforms](https://mui.com/material-ui/getting-started/supported-platforms/), [MCP scope](https://mui.com/material-ui/getting-started/mcp/).

**Tamagui** — This is one of my strongest alternatives for genuinely shared React/web and React Native UI. Its optional compiler extracts atomic CSS and flattens components, while `Adapt` can move a Select or Popover into a Sheet without duplicating content or open state. That solves real cross-platform presentation work, but I did not establish a built-in runtime agent discovery/authorization contract from the sources I reviewed. I would pair its components with a constrained action/state interface and test accessibility on each target; if shared React implementation mattered more than framework-neutral agent interoperability, I could prefer it. [Core/compiler architecture](https://tamagui.dev/docs/intro/introduction), [Adapt’s state-preserving handoff](https://tamagui.dev/ui/adapt).

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — This is a focused React design system: Tailwind 4 tokens, Radix-based accessible components, dark-mode utilities, and ChatGPT-oriented styling. The UI package should not be confused with the surrounding MCP server and host integration: installing its components alone does not establish tool permissions or a native widget layer. I would use it for an interface intended to feel at home inside ChatGPT, but not as the common implementation for standalone web, SwiftUI, and Android screens. A separate host bridge and platform-specific renderers would be required. [Package architecture and prerequisites](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui), [host/server UI integration](https://developers.openai.com/apps-sdk/build/chatgpt-ui).

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — `MaterialTheme` propagates color, typography, and shape into Compose components, including dynamic color and Material 3 Expressive support. Compose semantics are especially valuable: roles, state descriptions, and actions are consumed by accessibility services and the testing framework, not merely painted on screen. That is a strong Android foundation, but it is not itself a platform-neutral agent tool contract or a shared web implementation. I would retain it beneath an Android adapter—A2UI documents one—while implementing authorization outside the UI and verifying protocol-version compatibility rather than assuming Android’s renderer supports every web feature. [Material implementation](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3), [semantic actions and testing](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/accessibility/semantics), [A2UI renderer versions](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/).

**Radix UI** — Radix Primitives provide low-level React web interactions with documented WAI-ARIA behavior, keyboard support, and focus management. I value that AlertDialog anticipates safe focus placement, but application authors must still supply labels and preserve correct composition. These are dependable building blocks for human-facing controls, not native widgets or a runtime agent operation schema. Styling, explicit application tools, and native renderers would address my objections; I would use Radix beneath that architecture rather than ask it to provide those unrelated layers. [Accessibility behavior and author responsibilities](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/overview/accessibility).

**Chakra UI** — Chakra supplies accessible React web components and a configurable styling system built around tokens, semantic tokens, recipes, and slot recipes. Its MCP server exposes component props, examples, theme information, and migration assistance, which is useful authoring support but distinct from agents using the deployed product. I would choose it for rapid, cohesive web development, not as the entire native-and-agent interface architecture. Native renderers and a shared runtime action layer would close that scope gap; custom token changes also need the documented type-generation step to keep typings synchronized. [Theming architecture](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/theming/overview), [MCP tools](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/get-started/ai/mcp-server).

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — Its best idea directly addresses the brief: `defineAction` is shared by UI hooks, agent tools, HTTP, MCP, A2A, and CLI, with common validation, access checks, and auditing. Shared database data and relevant application state avoid the fragile pattern of making an agent click through a separate interface. The trade-off is adopting a much broader TypeScript application framework, including server and data conventions, rather than selecting a portable presentation toolkit; the reviewed sources do not establish native widget parity. I would favor it for a new full-stack agent application, but require demonstrated native clients and a plan for integrating existing infrastructure before choosing it here. [Shared action architecture](https://agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview), [included runtime and data stack](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native).

**MCP Apps** — This is an interoperability and embedding layer, not a visual design system. Tools reference `ui://` HTML resources, compliant hosts render them in sandboxed iframes, and JSON-RPC carries tool data and UI requests; the stable specification also defines CSP and permissions metadata. I would choose it for distributing an interactive tool across compliant chat hosts, but HTML in a native host is still not SwiftUI or Compose rendering, and host capability support varies. Pairing it with an accessible component system and testing every target host addresses deployment concerns; genuinely native rendering requires another layer. [Stable specification and security model](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx), [host support caveat](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps).

**A2UI** — My choice is its separation of catalog-constrained UI data, shared protocol/state cores, and framework-specific native rendering. Incremental component/data updates, two-way bindings, typed function RPCs, `allowedCallers`, and `requiresUserActivation` let me distinguish agent composition from authorized operation and direct human gestures. Coverage is concrete but not uniform: the SDK matrix lists web, Flutter, and SwiftUI v1.0 support, while Jetpack Compose is listed at v0.9.1; SwiftUI also documents group-hint, live-region text, and older-OS subtree-reset limitations. I would negotiate capabilities, maintain a tested common catalog, and keep authentication, business authorization, and consequential-action confirmation in trusted handlers—schema validation is not a replacement for them. [SDK/version matrix](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/), [function permissions](https://a2ui.org/concepts/actions-and-functions/), [native implementation and limitations](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/blob/main/swift/swiftui/README.md).

**Ouro UI** — This is unusually close to a complete human-and-agent design system: Base UI-backed copy-in web controls, a SwiftUI companion, typed outcomes, and an external AX X-ray. Its one action model generates CLI, MCP, WebMCP, web controls, App Intents, SwiftUI buttons, and Reins declarations, with consent classes and CI drift checking; that is more explicit action-surface engineering than I get from A2UI alone. I did not choose it because Android and Windows kits are explicitly unimplemented and the Apple companion remains pre-1.0, not because it lacks an agent architecture. Stable native coverage beyond Apple and independently exercised end-to-end flows would address my objection; its own X-ray documentation correctly distinguishes conformance from successful task flows. [Action generation and consent](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md), [platform gaps](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/README.md), [external testing and limits](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md), [Apple status](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-apple).

**Flutter** — Flutter offers the broadest straightforward single-rendering-stack alternative: mobile, web, and desktop from Dart, with Material and Cupertino widgets. I would not dismiss its web output as inaccessible canvas: the documented semantics layer translates roles into accessible HTML, though it must be enabled and custom widgets need proper semantics. Agent-driven composition is also available through GenUI’s widget catalog and state-feedback loop, but that SDK is explicitly alpha. I would choose Flutter for a greenfield application committed to its rendering stack; I prefer A2UI here because it also accommodates existing DOM, SwiftUI, and Compose applications without requiring a Flutter rewrite. [Platform/rendering architecture](https://github.com/flutter/flutter), [web semantics](https://docs.flutter.dev/ui/accessibility/web-accessibility), [GenUI architecture and alpha status](https://docs.flutter.dev/ai/genui).

**AI Elements** — Its copy-in React components solve the presentation of conversations, tool calls, reasoning, and approvals, rather than the underlying agent execution contract. There is also a cutoff-relevant migration: the repository announces deprecation at the end of November 2026, while the fetched shadcn documentation already provides replacement patterns and migration guidance, with existing copied code continuing to work. I would use those current patterns for a web chat surface, not start a new dependency strategy around the retiring project. Native presentation, persistent shared state, and enforced tool authorization still need other layers. [Repository migration notice](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements), [current replacements and migration details](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/ai-elements).

**CopilotKit** — This is a strong runtime-oriented contender: AG-UI streams connect agents to shared state, frontend tools, generative UI, and human-in-the-loop workflows. Native support is real rather than hypothetical: its React Native package offers headless hooks and optional chat components, but native generative UI is explicitly experimental and the quickstart documents significant Metro/polyfill setup, including security-sensitive random-source import order. I would choose it when embedding an operational copilot in an existing React-family product, and it can complement A2UI rather than replace it. I prefer A2UI as the common rendering contract across non-React native frameworks; mature native generative-UI coverage would narrow that distinction. [Runtime architecture](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit), [shared state](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/shared-state), [native implementation and caveats](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/react-native).

**json-render** — Its `defineCatalog`/`defineRegistry` split, Zod-defined props, SpecStream JSON Patch updates, and React Native renderer make it a serious cross-platform alternative, not merely a web JSON demo. The native renderer documents standard controls, action providers, two-way bindings, and an externally controlled `StateStore`, so application and agent updates can share state without regenerating executable code. I prefer A2UI’s documented SwiftUI/Compose adapters and explicit caller/user-activation permissions; I did not establish equivalent standardized caller authority from the json-render sources reviewed. I would enforce action authorization in trusted handlers and test catalog/accessibility parity across renderers rather than treat schema-conforming output as guaranteed usable or safe behavior. [Catalog and streaming architecture](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/core/README.md), [native renderer and controlled state](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/react-native/README.md).

reviews.pullQuote: I would choose A2UI: a catalog-constrained interface contract that gives agents structured state and operations while people use native-framework controls.
reviews.testimonial: I would choose A2UI as the common interface contract rather than force every platform into one renderer. Its Basic Catalog, incremental updateDataModel messages, and bidirectional Function RPC connect human controls with explicit agent operations. Compared with Tamagui, I give up a simpler shared React component implementation and take on catalog mapping and protocol-version negotiation. I would keep authorization in the application and gate deployment on platform-specific accessibility and conformance tests.
reviews.evaluations:
**AI Elements** — This is a copy-in React presentation layer for AI applications, not a cross-platform interaction contract. Conversation, Reasoning, Tool, and the [Confirmation component](https://elements.ai-sdk.dev/components/confirmation) make streaming output and approval states understandable, but execution policy still belongs to the application and AI SDK. More decisively, the [captured README](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements) announces deprecation at the end of November 2026 and migration to shadcn/ui. I would use the successor for a web chat surface, not start a new foundational dependency here; native rendering and shared agent operations would require another layer.

**Tamagui** — My strongest alternative for a conventional shared web/mobile component system. Its [compiler architecture](https://github.com/tamagui/tamagui/blob/main/code/tamagui.dev/data/docs/intro/introduction.mdx) turns style props or Tailwind utilities into atomic CSS on web and native styles on iOS/Android, with runtime fallback rather than a mandatory compilation cliff. [Select](https://tamagui.dev/ui/select) shares selection state across floating web lists, native HTML controls, and adapted Sheets while documenting platform differences. That is substantive portability, not merely responsive CSS. I would still need to add a discoverable, permissioned agent-operation contract; pairing its components with such a contract would address my main objection, but A2UI supplies that shared vocabulary directly.

**Vercel UI SDK** — The framework-free behavior core, definePrimitive, and five web adapters separate interaction logic from rendering effectively. Crucially, [createAgent](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent) lets agents inspect state and invoke component APIs, rather than merely helping them generate code. Its [permissions model](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent/permissions) includes allow callbacks, confirmation markers, secret redaction, and cancelable changes. However, multi-step actions are not transactions, and API invocation bypasses keyboard/pointer-handler checks. The published adapters are web adapters and the project is beta. I would want a native adapter, explicit backend authorization, and transaction-aware domain operations before choosing it as the cross-platform foundation.

**Base UI** — A strong unstyled React foundation with compound parts, focus behavior, portals, and freedom over visual design. Its [render-prop composition model](https://base-ui.com/react/handbook/composition) specifies event ordering, ref composition, and prop merging, which helps make wrappers predictable. The [quick start](https://base-ui.com/react/overview/quick-start) also documents real integration requirements such as portal stacking and iOS Safari backdrops. I would choose it underneath a branded web catalog, but it does not itself provide the native renderer or shared agent-operation protocol I need. Native implementations and an explicit action/catalog layer would address that architectural boundary; LLM-readable documentation alone does not.

**json-render** — A close contender: defineCatalog constrains components and actions, defineRegistry supplies implementations, and SpecStream incrementally builds JSON specifications. Its [React Native package](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/react-native/README.md) has actual native components, two-way bindings, an external StateStore, and action dispatch—not just a mobile roadmap. The [native ActionProvider source](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/react-native/src/contexts/actions.tsx) also implements pending confirmations. I prefer A2UI's documented SwiftUI/Compose integration and negotiated cross-language protocol over centering the contract on json-render's JavaScript ecosystem. Catalog constraints and optional confirmation metadata still need application-owned authorization, audited component implementations, and cross-renderer behavior tests.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — The [library architecture](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui) is well targeted: React components built on Radix, Tailwind 4-integrated tokens, dark-mode utilities, and ChatGPT-oriented styling. Its [responsive-design guide](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui/blob/main/src/Responsive%20design.mdx) provides consistent breakpoints and a useBreakpoint hook. I would choose it for visual integration inside ChatGPT, but distinguish this UI package from the surrounding Apps SDK's tool transport and host APIs. Responsive web components do not become native controls simply because their host runs on a phone. A host-independent action contract and separate native implementations would be needed for the broader brief.

**shadcn/ui** — Its [open-code and registry architecture](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs) gives developers—and coding agents—editable component implementations instead of increasingly complicated wrapper layers. The [MCP server](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/mcp) supports discovering and installing registry items, which is valuable build-time tooling but is not a runtime API for operating the finished application. I would use shadcn/ui to create the web implementation of a controlled component catalog. Copy-in ownership also means owning local modifications and reconciling upstream fixes. A shared action contract, native implementations, and automated upgrade/accessibility tests would close the gaps that keep it from being my single cross-platform choice.

**Ouro UI** — This is unusually serious about distinguishing interfaces people use from interfaces agents use. The [one action model](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md) generates CLI, MCP, WebMCP, web-control, App Intent, and SwiftUI surfaces, with consent classes and CI drift checks; [Ouro AX](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax.md) adds typed outcomes, receipts, postconditions, and external conformance checks. The Base UI-backed web components also have a documented [screen-reader test lane](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/screen-reader-lane.md), including candid known findings. I did not choose it because the [Apple package](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-apple) remains pre-1.0 with a narrower component set, while Android and Windows remain open platform work in the main README. Stable native parity and independent adoption evidence would substantially strengthen its case.

**Chakra UI** — Its [createSystem architecture](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/theming/overview), semantic tokens, recipes, slot recipes, and strictTokens option provide a useful enforceable styling vocabulary for a web product. The [MCP server](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/get-started/ai/mcp-server) exposes component props, examples, theme information, and migration guidance to coding agents. I value that practical authoring support, but it should not be confused with agents invoking application capabilities at runtime. The reviewed package is a React web system, with Emotion in its installation stack, rather than a native renderer. I would need native component implementations and a permissioned state/action layer; A2UI makes that latter contract the foundation rather than an application-specific addition.

**MUI** — A compelling choice for a React web application needing extensive ready-made controls and a consistent theme. [ThemeProvider and createTheme](https://mui.com/material-ui/customization/theming/) centralize component overrides and can generate CSS theme variables; the [official MCP server](https://mui.com/material-ui/getting-started/mcp/) supplies current documentation and examples to coding assistants. The Material UI implementation is separate from Android's Material 3 toolkit, so visual-family similarity does not provide shared native components or actions. I would use MUI as a web renderer implementation, with validated theme inputs and explicit backend operations. Shared catalog mappings to native toolkits would address portability, but would be work outside MUI itself.

**A2UI** — My choice for the shared interface contract. Core SDKs maintain component graphs and reactive data; Agent SDKs negotiate catalogs and validate generated output; renderer adapters map that state into host-framework views. The [current protocol](https://a2ui.org/specification/v1.0-a2ui/) adds typed bidirectional Function RPC, while the [action model](https://a2ui.org/concepts/actions-and-functions/) distinguishes user events, direct functions, and caller restrictions. These are implemented concepts, not just aspirations: the repository includes an [RPC handler](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/blob/main/typescript/core/web_core/src/rpc/rpc-handler.ts) and language-independent conformance cases. I would initially use v1.0 on React and Flutter. The [integration guide](https://a2ui.org/guides/client-integration/) explicitly identifies Compose's alpha renderer as v0.9.1, so I would not assume v1 RPC parity there; the [SwiftUI adapter](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/blob/main/swift/swiftui/README.md) also documents accessibility limitations. Version negotiation, native accessibility testing, curated catalogs, and server-side authorization remain my responsibilities. I accept that work to avoid coupling the contract to one visual system or host.

**MCP Apps** — The [stable specification](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx) standardizes ui:// resources, tool-to-UI linkage, bidirectional JSON-RPC, sandboxed HTML, and host-enforced content security policy. This is an excellent distribution boundary for interactive tool results across compliant agent hosts, and more interoperable than a bespoke iframe bridge. However, HTML resources and host-dependent capabilities are not native widget rendering or a complete design system. I would adopt it to distribute an interface built with my chosen catalog, while retaining a structured-data fallback and testing host permissions. Native rendering would need an additional adapter or content format, rather than being something I assume the current specification supplies.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — For an Apple-first product, [SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui) provides declarative state-driven views, adaptive controls, and UIKit/AppKit integration, while the [HIG accessibility guidance](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility) supplies concrete requirements for Dynamic Type, contrast, and inspection. The adjacent [App Intents framework](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appintents) genuinely exposes structured actions and entities to system experiences; I would not overlook that agent-facing capability. My objection is platform scope, not native quality. Web and Android require other renderers, and arbitrary external agents need another access boundary. A shared catalog and action contract would preserve SwiftUI's strengths without making Apple's frameworks the universal contract.

**Fluent UI** — Fluent is broader than the supplied web repository: its [development guide](https://fluent2.microsoft.design/get-started/develop) covers React, Web Components, Apple, Android, and Windows, and the [Android repository](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui-android) includes Kotlin/Compose controls. React v9 uses FluentProvider and Griffel; other platforms have their own implementations and release paths. I would choose it for a Microsoft-aligned product family, but cross-platform design-language consistency is not one shared implementation or agent-operation schema. I would add catalog adapters, shared domain-action definitions, and parity tests. Those measures address drift across implementations, but A2UI gives me the portable interface contract independently of Microsoft's visual language.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — [MaterialTheme](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3) combines color schemes, typography, and shapes, including dynamic color and Material 3 Expressive support. Compose's [semantics tree](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/accessibility/semantics) exposes roles, state, and actions to accessibility services and tests, providing more reliable interaction structure than pixels alone. There is also a real Compose A2UI integration, not merely a hypothetical one, though the [integration guide](https://a2ui.org/guides/client-integration/) documents its alpha/v0.9.1 boundary. I would choose this as my Android implementation, not as the web-and-native contract. Additional platform renderers and deliberate protocol-version handling address the scope mismatch.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — Its [shared-action architecture](https://agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview) is especially persuasive: defineAction routes UI hooks, agent tools, HTTP, MCP, A2A, and CLI calls through the same validation, access checks, and audit path. Shared SQL data and application context make humans and agents collaborators rather than separate integrations. Native reach exists, but is mixed: the [desktop shell](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native/blob/main/packages/desktop-app/README.md) embeds apps in Electron webviews, while the [mobile package](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native/blob/main/packages/mobile-app/README.md) documents an Expo/Xcode compile limitation and a narrower verification harness. I would consider it for the entire application runtime; for this choice, I prefer A2UI's smaller renderer-independent contract. Verified production mobile builds and accepting its broader backend/runtime architecture would resolve my main reservations.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — My preferred web accessibility baseline among the conventional component foundations. The [library split](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum) separates unstyled React Aria behavior, React Stately state, internationalization utilities, and Spectrum's styled system. Its [quality documentation](https://react-spectrum.adobe.com/react-aria/accessibility.html) specifies screen-reader testing, keyboard/focus handling, multilingual support, and normalized pointer interactions. That structure benefits human users and semantic browser automation, but automation-friendly DOM is not itself a permissioned domain API. React Stately's portability also should not be mistaken for native React Aria controls. I would preserve this foundation inside a web catalog and add native implementations plus explicit agent actions; A2UI supplies the cross-platform contract those implementations can share.

**CopilotKit** — A very strong alternative when integrating an existing agent is the central job. [Shared State](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/shared-state) uses AG-UI snapshots/deltas to synchronize application and agent state, while frontend tools and human-in-the-loop hooks support actual collaboration. Its [React Native package](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit/blob/main/packages/react-native/README.md) re-exports platform-agnostic hooks through a headless entry point; I would not describe it as web-only. Native generative UI is explicitly experimental and has a release-version caveat, however. I prefer A2UI for the narrower catalog/rendering contract across different native frameworks, rather than adopting CopilotKit's runtime integration as the foundation. Pinning compatible packages, verifying native polyfills, and supplying a coherent component system would make CopilotKit a credible application-level choice.

**Flutter** — The [SDK](https://github.com/flutter/flutter) offers substantial web, mobile, and desktop reuse through Dart, its own rendering engine, and Material/Cupertino widgets. Agent-oriented composition also exists through the [GenUI SDK](https://docs.flutter.dev/ai/genui), although that orchestration package is explicitly alpha. The important web trade-off is concrete: Flutter draws the visual UI on canvas and exposes an accessibility DOM through its Semantics tree; [web accessibility is opt-in by default](https://docs.flutter.dev/ui/accessibility/web-accessibility). I would explicitly enable semantics and test roles, focus, and browser automation rather than calling Flutter inaccessible. It is an excellent A2UI renderer, but I prefer not to require every web and native client to adopt Flutter's rendering architecture.

**Radix UI** — A capable incremental foundation for accessible React web controls, with unstyled primitives and flexible composition. The [asChild contract](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/guides/composition) lets behavior attach to application-owned elements, but requires correct prop spreading, ref forwarding, and preservation of focusable semantics. Those requirements matter when agents generate wrappers: a component can look right while silently breaking interaction. I would use Radix within a tested web component catalog, not treat it as a native toolkit or agent-action protocol. Wrapper conformance tests, native counterparts, and an application-owned authorization/action layer would address the missing layers, which is why I choose A2UI as the shared contract instead.
