reviews.pullQuote: I would choose A2UI for its portable, catalog-constrained approach to interfaces that agents compose and people use.
reviews.testimonial: I would choose A2UI because its catalog-based rendering and streamed surface updates let the same agent-driven experience reach web and native frameworks without shipping executable UI code. Its two-way data binding and action events give people a way to collaborate with the agent, while host applications retain control over components. Compared with CopilotKit, I would need to assemble more of the chat, orchestration, and approval experience myself. I would also explicitly plan for the current Android protocol-version gap and enforce authorization outside the UI protocol.
reviews.evaluations:
**MUI** — Material UI provides a mature React component library and a `ThemeProvider` with palette, typography, and CSS-variable customization. It is a strong web design-system layer, but a cross-platform agent experience would still need native components and an agent interface; I would use it as an A2UI web catalog implementation rather than the common architecture. [MUI theming](https://mui.com/material-ui/customization/theming/).

**Flutter** — Flutter supplies Material and Cupertino widgets across mobile, desktop, and web, and its GenUI SDK composes an existing widget catalog into agent-driven UI. That is attractive for a Flutter-first product, but GenUI is documented as alpha and Flutter’s web accessibility uses a semantics layer; A2UI lets me retain other host frameworks instead. [Flutter GenUI](https://docs.flutter.dev/ai/genui).

**CopilotKit** — AG-UI streams, shared state, frontend tools, and human-in-the-loop flows make it a particularly strong application-integration choice; it can also render A2UI and MCP Apps. I prefer A2UI as the more framework-independent UI contract, though CopilotKit offers more ready-made orchestration and chat; its React Native generative-UI entry point is documented as experimental. [React Native quickstart](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/react-native).

**Base UI** — Unstyled React primitives provide accessible interaction behavior, and the `render` prop composes it onto custom DOM elements. It gives a web team precise design control but leaves styling, agent communication, and native surfaces to other layers; it would work well underneath an A2UI web catalog. [Composition guide](https://base-ui.com/react/handbook/composition).

**Fluent UI** — The web repository offers React v9 and Web Components, while a separate Fluent UI React Native project targets multiple native platforms. That makes it a plausible cross-platform design system, but the native project describes its platform implementations as alpha; agent communication and per-platform component parity would also need integration. [Fluent UI React Native](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui-react-native).

**A2UI** — Its protocol separates streamed component updates from a data model, while catalogs and framework adapters map approved components to host UI; actions and two-way bindings connect user interactions back to the agent. I would add a host design system, server-side authorization, confirmation for consequential actions, and accessibility tests: a schema alone does not guarantee safe or usable outcomes. The documented Jetpack Compose renderer supports v0.9.1, whereas web, Flutter, and SwiftUI list v1.0, so version negotiation or an Android-compatible fallback is necessary. [SDK and renderer versions](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/).

**MCP Apps** — An MCP tool points to a `ui://` HTML resource that a host renders in a sandboxed iframe, with bidirectional JSON-RPC communication. It is excellent for distributing interactive tools into compatible agent hosts, but its initial HTML-based model and host-dependent support are different from rendering platform-native components inside my own apps; I would add it when host distribution matters. [MCP Apps specification](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx).

**Vercel UI SDK** — Framework-neutral behaviors compose into web primitives, while `createAgent` exposes component snapshots, queries, and actions, with permission hooks and optional WebMCP registration. This directly supports agents operating existing controls, but the listed adapters are web frameworks and the SDK is beta; I would need native equivalents and cross-platform contracts. [Agent bridge](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent).

**AI Elements** — Copy-in React components such as Tool, Message, and Reasoning make agent activity legible to people, but they are presentation patterns rather than a cross-platform agent-to-UI protocol. The repository announces deprecation at the end of November 2026 in favor of shadcn/ui’s version, so I would use the successor for a web chat layer instead. [AI Elements repository](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements).

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — Tailwind 4 tokens and styled React components built on Radix are useful for a consistent ChatGPT app. They do not themselves provide a native cross-platform interface or the MCP transport; I would use them for a ChatGPT-specific MCP App, not as the shared foundation. [Apps SDK UI](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui).

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — `defineAction` exposes one implementation through UI hooks, agent tools, HTTP, MCP, A2A, and CLI, with shared validation and access checks. That is a compelling answer to agents and people performing the same operations, but the documented React application layer is not itself a native UI system; I would consider its action architecture alongside native clients. [Actions overview](https://agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview).

**Radix UI** — Unstyled React primitives handle interaction and accessibility details, and `asChild` composes their behavior onto custom elements. It is a useful web catalog substrate, but it does not supply the cross-platform agent protocol; custom children must also forward props and refs and preserve accessible semantics. [Radix composition](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/guides/composition).

**Chakra UI** — Its React component system and `defineConfig`/`createSystem` theming support semantic tokens, recipes, and typed theme generation. That accelerates web product work, but I would still need native renderers and a runtime agent contract; its coding-agent documentation support is not the same thing as exposing application actions to an agent. [Chakra theming](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/theming/overview).

**json-render** — Typed catalogs, registries, streaming specs, and a React Native renderer make it a serious alternative; its native package includes standard controls and state bindings, while web has a prebuilt shadcn catalog. I favor A2UI’s documented SwiftUI and Compose adapters and transport specification for independently implemented native hosts; json-render is especially attractive when React Native is the mobile target. [React Native renderer](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/react-native/README.md).

**Tamagui** — Shared tokens and composable React/React Native components, plus a compiler that extracts web CSS and flattens eligible trees, make it a strong human-facing universal design system. It does not by itself establish the agent UI exchange I want, so I would pair it with an agent layer if a React Native codebase were the priority. [Tamagui architecture](https://tamagui.dev/docs/intro/introduction).

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — `MaterialTheme` supplies color, typography, and shapes, including Android dynamic color, and is a strong native Android design foundation. It is not the whole web-and-native strategy; I would use its A2UI Compose integration for Android while accounting for the currently documented v0.9.1 protocol support. [Material 3 in Compose](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3).

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — React Aria separates unstyled accessible behavior from presentation, React Stately supplies state, and Spectrum supplies Adobe-styled components; the project documents screen-reader testing and internationalization. These are excellent web foundations, but native rendering and agent interaction require additional layers, even though React Stately can be reused independently on other platforms. [React Aria quality](https://react-spectrum.adobe.com/react-aria/accessibility.html).

**Ouro UI** — Ouro combines copy-in Base UI-based web components with an Apple SwiftUI package, and its one-action generator produces web controls, MCP tools, App Intents, and other surfaces with drift checks. That is unusually well aligned with both people and agents, but the Apple package is pre-1.0, its component set is limited, and the project identifies Android as open for a builder; broader platform coverage and parity would strengthen its case. [Ouro UI](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui).

**shadcn/ui** — Its open-code approach copies components into the application, and its registry distributes components and other files; the current AI Elements patterns add chat, tool, and confirmation presentations. Ownership and customization are strengths, but I would still need native implementations and an agent interaction protocol, so I would use it as a web catalog rather than the common cross-platform contract. [Registry documentation](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/registry).

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — SwiftUI provides declarative views, controls, data flow, accessibility customization, and adaptation across Apple platforms; the HIG supplies platform design guidance. This is a strong Apple client foundation but not a web or Android solution, so I would use it through a SwiftUI renderer and expose platform actions separately. [SwiftUI documentation](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui).
candidateOrder: SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines

reviews.evaluations:
**A2UI** — A2UI separates agent inference, wire transport, and client rendering into three conformance-tested layers: Core SDKs (`@a2ui/web_core`, `a2ui-core`, `a2ui_core`, `A2UISwiftCore`, `androidx.a2ui`), Agent SDKs (`@a2ui/agent`, `a2ui-agent-sdk`, `a2ui_agent`), and native Renderer SDKs for React, Lit, Angular, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose ([A2UI SDKs](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/), [a2ui-project/a2ui](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui)). Because agents emit schema-validated JSON payloads rather than executable code, hosts enforce strict trust boundaries while streaming incremental updates and mapping accessibility attributes to native APIs without WebViews. Its main trade-offs are that it relies on the host framework's own theming rather than shipping a complete brand design system, and its Jetpack Compose renderer (`v0.9.1`) trails the `v1.0` releases of SwiftUI, Flutter, and Web; pairing A2UI with a runtime like CopilotKit or native platform catalogs addresses app-shell and session management.

**CopilotKit** — CopilotKit provides an end-to-end stack connecting agent backends (LangGraph, CrewAI, Mastra, Google ADK, PydanticAI) over the AG-UI protocol to React/Next.js, Angular, Vue, React Native, and chat channels like Slack and Microsoft Teams ([CopilotKit/CopilotKit](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit)). It uniquely unifies three generative UI modes—controlled AG-UI tool calls, declarative A2UI 1.0 specs, and sandboxed MCP Apps—alongside shared state, human-in-the-loop approvals, and WebMCP. Its native mobile coverage is limited to React Native rather than native SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose, or Flutter, and production features like Continual Learning and persistent threads center on CopilotKit Intelligence; adding first-class SwiftUI and Compose SDKs would close the native gap.

**Ouro UI** — Ouro UI pairs human-facing copy-in components (`Ouro HX`, built on Base UI and Tailwind v4 on web, and `OuroHX` in SwiftUI on Apple) with agent-facing interfaces (`Ouro AX`) and a single TypeScript declaration model (`ouro-ui-core`) that generates CLI commands, MCP/WebMCP tools, web controls, Apple App Intents, and `OuroReins` screen-driving actions ([ourostack/ouro-ui](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui), [ourostack/ouro-ui-apple](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-apple)). It also ships `OuroA2UI` to render A2UI surfaces in SwiftUI with consent-checked actions. However, its Apple package is pre-1.0 (`v0.4.x`), Android and Windows remain unbuilt ("open for a builder"), and its web layer is tied to React 19, Base UI, and Tailwind CSS v4; shipping Android/Compose and cross-framework web support would make it a universal contender.

**json-render** — json-render is a generative UI framework that constrains LLM output to Zod-defined component catalogs and streams JSON or YAML specs to renderers across React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, React Native, Next.js, TanStack Start, Remotion, PDF, Email, Ink, Three.js, Slack/Teams/Discord, and MCP Apps ([vercel-labs/json-render](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render)). Its breadth of non-DOM targets (terminal, video, email, 3D) is unmatched in the TypeScript ecosystem. Its trade-off is that native mobile is limited to React Native—there are no native SwiftUI or Jetpack Compose renderers—and it lacks an agent-user session protocol like AG-UI or native OS intent bindings; adding Swift/Kotlin renderers would bridge native platforms.

**MCP Apps** — MCP Apps extends the Model Context Protocol so tools can declare `ui://` HTML resources that host clients (Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code, Goose, Postman) render inline inside sandboxed iframes with bidirectional `PostMessageTransport` communication ([modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps)). This gives tool authors portable, zero-install interactive UIs across compliant chat hosts. By design, however, it is an iframe-based web embedding standard rather than a native SwiftUI/Compose/Flutter toolkit or a standalone application design system, and host support varies across clients; native host renderers or pairing with A2UI (`@a2ui/catalog-mcp`) addresses native fidelity.

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — Agent-native is a TypeScript framework where capabilities are defined once via `defineAction` and exposed simultaneously to React (`useActionQuery`), agent tools, HTTP, MCP, A2A, and CLI, backed by shared PostgreSQL/PGlite state and `/visual-edit` workflows ([BuilderIO/agent-native](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native)). This eliminates drift between what the agent and the human UI can do. Its observed scope is TypeScript/React web applications with no native mobile UI renderers or cross-platform design tokens; adding native client SDKs would be required for iOS/Android.

**Vercel UI SDK** — Vercel UI SDK (`@ui-sdk/core`) packages interaction behaviors—keyboard navigation, focus recovery, selection, popups, drag and drop, and ARIA—into framework-agnostic primitives with `createParts` adapters for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and Web Components, accompanied by an agent skill for coding agents ([vercel-labs/ui](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui)). Its behavior-first architecture is clean and portable across web frameworks, though it is currently in beta. It is web-only with no native mobile adapters, and its agent story targets *coding agents authoring UI* rather than runtime agent-user interaction; adding native adapters and runtime agent protocols would address both gaps.

**Tamagui** — Tamagui combines `@tamagui/core`, an optimizing compiler (`@tamagui/static`) that flattens styled components to atomic CSS on web and hoisted views on React Native, and a universal UI kit ([tamagui/tamagui](https://github.com/tamagui/tamagui)). It is one of the strongest code-sharing toolkits across React web and React Native without sacrificing runtime performance. However, Tamagui is a human-authored UI and styling system rather than an agentic interface protocol, and it does not target non-React native stacks like SwiftUI or Flutter; pairing it with CopilotKit or json-render on React Native would add agentic UI capabilities.

**Flutter** — Flutter compiles Dart to ARM machine code, JavaScript/WebAssembly, and desktop binaries, rendering pixel-consistent Material and Cupertino widgets via Skia and Impeller from a single codebase ([flutter/flutter](https://github.com/flutter/flutter)). As a cross-platform rendering engine across mobile, web, and desktop, it is mature and fast. By itself, Flutter has no built-in agent protocol, catalog validation, or generative UI runtime, which is why A2UI ships `a2ui_flutter` on top of it; pairing Flutter with A2UI directly resolves the agent-interface gap.

**shadcn/ui** — shadcn/ui distributes open-code React web components built on Tailwind CSS and accessible primitives (Radix/Base UI) that you copy directly into your codebase ([shadcn-ui/ui](https://github.com/shadcn-ui/ui)). It has become the de facto web component base for AI coding agents and is absorbing Vercel's AI Elements patterns. It is, however, web-only (no first-party native mobile implementation) and provides static human UI components rather than a runtime agent-UI protocol; using it as the web rendering layer behind `json-render` (`@json-render/shadcn`) or A2UI addresses agentic composition.

**Base UI** — Base UI (`@base-ui/react`) delivers unstyled, accessible web React primitives from the creators of Radix, Floating UI, and Material UI ([mui/base-ui](https://github.com/mui/base-ui)). It gives teams full styling control and solid ARIA behavior on the web, and serves as the foundation for libraries like Ouro HX. Because it is strictly web React with no React Native or native mobile support and no built-in agent protocol, it would need a cross-platform wrapper and an agentic layer like A2UI or CopilotKit.

**Radix UI** — Radix Primitives provides low-level, accessible, unstyled React web components designed for incremental adoption ([radix-ui/primitives](https://github.com/radix-ui/primitives)). Its battle-tested focus management and keyboard handling underpin many web systems (including OpenAI Apps SDK UI and shadcn/ui). Like Base UI, it is web-only and human-centric, lacking native mobile targets and runtime agent-UI primitives; pairing it with web generative UI frameworks addresses agent composition on the web only.

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — Adobe's React Spectrum ecosystem separates state hooks (`React Stately`), unstyled accessible hooks/components (`React Aria`), and Adobe's design system (`React Spectrum`), with strong WAI-ARIA, pointer/touch/keyboard adaptation, and 30+ locale internationalization ([adobe/react-spectrum](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum)). While `React Stately` can be reused outside the DOM, `React Aria` and `React Spectrum` are web-focused and do not provide native iOS/Android UI renderers or agentic UI protocols; adding native platform adapters and an agent catalog layer would be needed for this prompt.

**Chakra UI** — Chakra UI (`@chakra-ui/react`) is an accessible React web component system supporting Next.js RSC and Emotion styling, and it publishes an official MCP server (`@chakra-ui/react-mcp`) so coding agents can query component docs, props, and tokens ([chakra-ui/chakra-ui](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui)). That MCP integration helps coding agents *build* with Chakra, but Chakra itself remains a web-only React library without native mobile renderers or runtime agent-driven UI composition.

**MUI** — Material UI (`@mui/material`) is a mature React web implementation of Google's Material Design, extended by MUI X for complex data grids and charts ([mui/material-ui](https://github.com/mui/material-ui)). It offers deep enterprise component coverage for web apps, but it is web-only and lacks native mobile renderers or built-in agentic UI protocols; teams needing native Material on Android and agentic UI would pair Jetpack Compose with A2UI instead.

**Fluent UI** — Microsoft's primary `fluentui` repository provides Fluent UI React v9, v8, and Web Components for web applications ([microsoft/fluentui](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui)), while separate Microsoft repositories handle Fluent UI React Native (currently alpha-stage, with early `packages/agentic` work). The linked web repo itself has no native mobile renderers and no built-in runtime agent-UI protocol like AG-UI or A2UI, limiting its fit for unified web-and-native agentic interfaces.

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — Apps SDK UI (`@openai/apps-sdk-ui`) is a lightweight React 18/19 and Tailwind 4 design system built on Radix primitives for rendering consistent experiences inside ChatGPT ([openai/apps-sdk-ui](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui)). Its tokens and components are well suited for ChatGPT-embedded web UIs, but it is React/web-only and tightly scoped to ChatGPT's host environment rather than standalone native apps or multi-host agentic architectures.

**AI Elements** — AI Elements provides shadcn/ui-based React components for Next.js AI apps (conversations, messages, reasoning, code blocks) ([vercel/ai-elements](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements)). Its repository explicitly warns that it will be deprecated at the end of November 2026 in favor of AI Elements inside `shadcn/ui`. Even after that move, it remains a Next.js/React web UI pattern library with no native mobile support or cross-platform generative UI protocol.

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — SwiftUI is Apple's declarative native UI framework across iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, visionOS, and watchOS ([SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui)), pairing with Apple's App Intents framework to expose structured app capabilities to Siri and system agents. It delivers the highest native fidelity on Apple hardware, but it is strictly locked to Apple platforms with no web, Android, or cross-platform agent protocol—which is why A2UI (`A2UISwiftUI`) and Ouro UI (`OuroHX`/`OuroAX`) build on top of it rather than replacing it.

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — Material 3 in Jetpack Compose is Android's declarative native UI toolkit and design system across phones, tablets, foldables, XR, Wear OS, TV, and Auto ([Material 3 in Compose](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3)), complemented by Android's experimental AppFunctions for exposing capabilities to agents like Gemini. Like SwiftUI on Apple, it is the gold standard for native Android fidelity, but it does not cover iOS or web—requiring a cross-platform protocol such as A2UI (`androidx.a2ui.compose` / `material3-a2ui`) to share agent-driven interfaces across platforms.
reviews.pullQuote: A2UI lets agents stream schema-validated, interactive interfaces that render directly as native SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose, Flutter, and web components—no WebViews required.
reviews.testimonial: I would choose A2UI because it is the only toolkit in this set engineered from the ground up for both people and agents across web and true native platforms. Its Core SDKs validate agent-generated UI against strict Catalog JSON Schemas and handle reactive data binding, while its official Renderer SDKs stream incremental surface updates directly into native SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose, Flutter, React, Lit, and Angular widget trees with host accessibility mapping. The honest trade-off compared to CopilotKit is that A2UI does not ship a full application shell, human-in-the-loop thread management, or a standalone visual design system—you pair it with your host platform's native theming or an orchestration layer when building a complete product.
candidateOrder: SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines

reviews.pullQuote: A2UI is the interface contract I would ship: one catalog, native widgets on web, SwiftUI, Flutter, and Compose, and no executable UI from the agent.
reviews.testimonial: I would build the shared interface on A2UI, not on a component library that hopes an agent can read the source. Catalog negotiation and updateComponents give the agent a streamable surface, and the renderer SDKs turn that surface into React, SwiftUI, Flutter, and Jetpack Compose widgets instead of an iframe. I still want Ouro UI’s consent classes: A2UI will render whatever button the catalog allows, so a person-only action has to be kept out of the catalog on purpose. The honest gap versus a finished design system is visual and versioned: host themes own the look, and the Compose renderer I checked is still on v0.9.1.
reviews.evaluations:
**A2UI** — This is the toolkit I would ship. An agent SDK compiles model output into v1.0 envelopes (`createSurface`, `updateComponents`, `updateDataModel`, `deleteSurface`); a renderer SDK maps the flat adjacency list onto host widgets. Catalog negotiation means the agent only emits component types the client advertised in `supportedCatalogIds`, never HTML or scripts. Official renderers I checked cover React, Lit, and Angular on v1.0, Flutter and SwiftUI on v1.0, and Jetpack Compose plus `material3-a2ui` only on v0.9.1. v1.0 removed theme from the wire, so the look stays with the host. Keeping person-only actions out of the catalog addresses the objection that the agent is composing UI rather than calling a stable product door; a v1.0 Compose renderer would close the Android skew. [SDKs](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/)

**Ouro UI** — The strongest design-system reading of the brief, and the one I would steal policy from. People get copy-in React on Base UI; agents get `defineCommand` surfaces (CLI, `--json`, MCP, typed outcomes) checked from outside by `ax-xray`. One action declaration is meant to generate the web control, MCP and WebMCP tools, a SwiftUI `Button(intent:)`, and Reins nodes, with CI failing on drift. Apple already has `OuroHX`, `OuroAX`, `OuroReins`, and `OuroA2UI`. I did not pick it because Android and Windows are documented as unbuilt, and the platforms table shows web meeting core v0.5.0 while Apple v0.5.0 still meets core v0.4.0. An Android kit projecting that same declaration onto AppFunctions and Compose, pinned to the same core, would answer that. [Decision record](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/decisions/2026-11-13-agents-use-agent-interfaces.md)

**json-render** — The closest generative alternative. `defineCatalog` constrains the model to Zod props and named actions; `Renderer` streams a spec into a registry you own. The repo documents React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, React Native, chat cards, PDF, email, Ink, and `@json-render/mcp`. The React Native package I read uses `@json-render/react-native/schema` and its own standard catalog (`Container`, `Button`, `TextInput`, `Modal`), not SwiftUI or Compose widgets. I would use it inside a web or React Native host, not as the cross-platform contract. One catalog schema implemented by those native UI frameworks would address that; I did not see that schema. [React Native renderer](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/f5c12405a19c45be5e0e90778ef888ed541b208f/packages/react-native/README.md)

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — `defineAction` is one validated implementation for the UI hook, the agent tool, HTTP, MCP, A2A, and CLI. That is the right action layer, and Ouro’s decision record cites it as the closest web-only prior art, without a parity check between a control and its tool. It is a TypeScript application framework, not a native renderer. A SwiftUI and Compose projection of `defineAction`, plus a generated-parity test, would address the objection. [README](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native)

**CopilotKit** — A runtime and chat shell, not the product surface. `CopilotRuntime` and `CopilotSidebar` sit on AG-UI, with shared state, human-in-the-loop, and frontend tools; the README lists React, Angular, Vue, React Native, Slack, and Teams. Setting `a2ui: {}` applies A2UI middleware and paints A2UI inside chat, so CopilotKit is a host for the protocol I would choose. I would not put native screens behind that chat renderer. First-class SwiftUI and Compose SDKs, rather than React Native and chat cards, would change the trade-off. [A2UI in CopilotKit](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/generative-ui/a2ui)

**MCP Apps** — SEP-1865, stable as of 2026-01-26, is the right distribution channel and the wrong app substrate. Tools declare `ui://` resources with mime type `text/html;profile=mcp-app`; hosts render them in a sandboxed iframe with CSP and JSON-RPC. That unifies ChatGPT Apps and MCP-UI for Claude, VS Code, and Goose. It does not render native widgets, and the spec’s initial content type is HTML. A non-HTML content type that hosts map onto native catalogs would address that; until then I would embed an MCP App inside an A2UI surface, which both projects already point at. [SEP-1865](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/ea3e9d0e624a20bc1c51310292f09d9b8ed17161/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx)

**Vercel UI SDK** — `@ui-sdk/core` is a behavior library (`definePrimitive`, slots, focus recovery) with adapters for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and Web Components. The agent path I fetched is runtime WebMCP: `registerTools` exposes `snapshot`, `act`, and `query` on `document.modelContext`, with an `allow` gate before `press`. That is how I would let a browser agent operate web controls. The install docs are web-only and the project is a public beta. The docs nav mentions a Platform Mobile section, but the mobile URLs I tried 404’d, so native-app support is unverified rather than disproven. A documented UIKit or Compose adapter would address the platform objection. [WebMCP](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent/webmcp)

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — Tailwind 4 tokens and React components on Radix, wrapped by `AppsSDKUIProvider`, for interfaces inside ChatGPT. It is a visual system for one host, not an agent protocol and not a native renderer. MCP Apps already took the protocol job this SDK helped motivate. Shipping the same tokens as a catalog a native host can implement would address the platform limit; styling ChatGPT cards does not. [README](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui)

**shadcn/ui** — A distribution system, not a runtime. Open code, a flat registry schema, and a CLI, with AI Elements now in the docs (`Message`, `Prompt Input`, `Tool`, `Chain of Thought`). Agents can read and edit the source, which is why it is a good place to keep web components. The docs I read do not define an agent wire protocol or a native target. A registry item that also emits an A2UI catalog would address the gap; copying React files does not. [Docs](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs)

**AI Elements** — shadcn-based chat pieces (`Conversation`, `Message`, `MessageResponse`) tied to the AI SDK and a Next.js plus Tailwind setup. The README says the project will be deprecated at the end of November 2026 and replaced by shadcn/ui’s AI Elements. I would not start a cross-platform system on a library with a published sunset date and no native renderer. Moving the components, which they are already doing, addresses the maintenance objection and still leaves the platform one. [README](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements)

**Tamagui** — The compiler flattens styled components to a `div` plus atomic CSS on web and a `View` with hoisted style objects on React Native, which is the best “one React tree, two runtimes” performance story here. There is no catalog, no action protocol, and no agent door in the README. I would use it as a renderer under a catalog, not as the language agents speak. An official A2UI or json-render catalog of Tamagui components would address that. [README](https://github.com/tamagui/tamagui)

**Flutter** — One codebase for iOS, Android, web, and desktop, with Material and Cupertino widgets and its own renderer. People get a real cross-platform UI. The Flutter repo itself does not give agents a UI protocol; `a2ui_flutter` is that piece and lives in the A2UI project. Choosing Flutter alone would force a WebView or a second protocol. Using Flutter as the A2UI host, which the v1.0 renderer already is, is how I would use it. [README](https://github.com/flutter/flutter)

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — Declarative views and scenes across iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, visionOS, and watchOS, with the HIG covering accessibility, layout, and platform adaptation, including iPhone Duo. This is what a person should feel on Apple, and App Intents are how Siri enters a third-party app, but neither document is a web toolkit or an agent UI protocol. I would implement an A2UI catalog with SwiftUI, not make SwiftUI the shared contract. A web renderer is not what would fix it; a protocol binding is, and that binding already exists outside this candidate. [SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui)

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — `MaterialTheme` color roles, a type scale, a shape scale, and tonal elevation, plus the Compose component set. That is the right visual system for Android, and `material3-a2ui` already exists as an A2UI catalog, on v0.9.1. Compose as documented here is not the web stack and not an agent protocol. Bringing that Material 3 catalog to A2UI v1.0 would be the fix, not adopting Compose as the multi-platform interface. [Material 3 in Compose](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3)

**MUI** — A long-maintained React implementation of Material Design, extended by MUI X. The README is a web component library with no agent catalog and no native renderer. I would not wrap that React surface and call it shared by agents on iOS and Android. A headless catalog export would be more useful than adopting `@mui/material` as the shared surface; Base UI is closer to that layer. [README](https://github.com/mui/material-ui)

**Base UI** — Unstyled accessible primitives from the Radix, Floating UI, and Material UI authors. Ouro HX is built on it (`--base base`), so it is the right headless layer for a web design system. It has no native renderer and no agent protocol in the README. Exposing each primitive’s state as a catalog component, the way UI SDK exposes behaviors, would address the agent half. [README](https://github.com/mui/base-ui)

**Radix UI** — Low-level accessible primitives, the historical base for shadcn/ui and for Apps SDK UI. Same architectural limit as Base UI: behavior without a cross-platform wire format. I would not pick both, and Base UI is the unstyled library in this set that a current design system here actually depends on. A maintained agent-facing state description per primitive would address the objection. [README](https://github.com/radix-ui/primitives)

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — React Aria implements WAI-ARIA behavior for mouse, touch, and keyboard, with internationalization; React Stately can be used independently, and the README notes that includes other platforms such as React Native. Spectrum itself is Adobe’s web design system. The behavior layer is excellent and still React-DOM-shaped for the components people import. A Stately-backed native catalog, not another styled web kit, is the piece I would take. [README](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum)

**Fluent UI** — Three web stacks in one repo: React v9 (`@fluentui/react-components`), React v8, and web components, with Griffel, slots, and theming, used by Microsoft 365 and Edge. I found no native renderer and no agent protocol in this repository. Adaptive Cards are a different Microsoft project, so I am not treating them as a capability of this candidate. A web-component catalog an agent can stream, plus a native projection, would address the gap. [README](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui)

**Chakra UI** — Accessible React components, Emotion, and Next.js RSC. The README’s MCP badge installs a docs server for a coding agent, which is not an end-user agent operating the product. It is web-only. An action catalog and a native renderer would address the brief; a documentation MCP does not. [README](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui)
candidateOrder: SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines
